# Guide to a Typeface That Arrives Late on the Web

This document explains why, on Compose Multiplatform's web target, an app's own typeface arrives a moment late, how we measured it and how we cured it. The problem is not Pantrix's own: it is seen the same way in **every** Compose Multiplatform project that has a web target and uses its own font file. Section 3 of the document gives the solution with Pantrix's API, section 4 without the library, in a form that can be copied into any project. 3.5 and 4.4 give a near problem of the same target too: Compose fetching a font from Google for a character the app's fonts lack.

## 1. The Problem

### Symptom

*   When the page is first opened in the browser, or reloaded, the text is first drawn in another typeface. Less than a second later all the letters change, the texts are laid out again and the lines shift.
*   When the typeface is changed while the app runs (in ours, "Typeface" in "Settings"), the same happens once more.
*   On Android, iOS and the desktop it is never seen.

On web pages this is called FOUT (*flash of unstyled text*).

### Cause

In Compose Multiplatform a font file is read with `Font(Res.font.…)`. This function does two separate things by platform (Compose Multiplatform 1.12.1, `components-resources`):

| Platform | Reading | In the first frame |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Android, iOS, desktop | Synchronous: the file is read the moment it is asked for (`ResourceState.blocking.kt`) | The typeface is ready |
| Web (`js`, `wasmJs`) | Asynchronous: the file is downloaded with `fetch` (`ResourceState.web.kt`) | There is no typeface |

On the web `Font(…)` returns a **fallback** until the file arrives: the Roboto that Skiko carries inside it (`FontResources.skiko.kt`, `defaultFont`). When the file arrives the value it returns changes, everything that reads it is set up again and every text is laid out again. Three details make the problem bigger:

1.  **The reading starts late.** `Font(…)` is a composable: the download starts only when the app is first being set up, that is, after the Wasm has been downloaded and compiled.
2.  **Every weight is a separate font.** The cache's key is the file's path, its weight, its style and its axis settings. A single variable font registered in seven weights is read seven times and can arrive at seven separate moments: the theme is set up from the start several times.
3.  **It is asked for again at every load.** The resources' cache in the browser (the Cache API) is reset at every page load (`ResourceWebCache.web.kt`); the file is given by the browser's own HTTP cache.

### Measurement

The production bundle (`wasmJsBrowserDistribution`) was opened from a local server; the times were read with a measuring script added to the page (see section 6). The numbers are milliseconds after the page opened.

| Event | Before the fix | After the fix |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| The typeface files were asked for | 408 (after the app was set up; only the theme's file) | 71 (while the code downloads, `<link rel="preload">`; all fifteen files) |
| All the fonts were read | 440 | 274 |
| The app's first frame | 401, **in the fallback typeface** | 456, **in its own typeface** |
| The letters changed | About 500 | Never |
| Another typeface was chosen in "Settings" | Seven files are asked for at that moment; the fallback typeface until they arrive | No new request; it changes in one frame |

Locally there is no network latency, and the difference is a hundred milliseconds; on a real network it lasts as long as the typeface is late. The first frame itself took between 175 and 240 ms in both measurements: waiting for the typeface did not delay the opening, because the files had come down long before that frame was set up.

## 2. The Solution: Four Pieces

| # | Piece | What it gives |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | **Download early.** `<link rel="preload">` in `index.html` | The file downloads while the app's code downloads; when the app asks for it, it is in the browser's cache |
| 2 | **Read first, draw after.** Put the app behind a gate | The app draws its first frame in its own typeface; the letters do not change |
| 3 | **Keep the loading mark.** Set up the app in its own box, not in the body | While waiting, the page's loading mark shows, not an empty page |
| 4 | **Stay with the old one when the typeface changes.** Change once, when the new one arrives | Changing the typeface while the app runs shows no fallback typeface either |

The second piece is the heart of the work, and rests on a property of Compose: **a font read stays in memory**, and the first setup that asks for it later finds it at once. So it is enough to ask for the typeface somewhere first (`preloadFont`) and to set up the app after that; nothing changes in the app itself.

## 3. With Pantrix

The library gives the Kotlin side of the four pieces (`com.pantrixui.foundation.token.typography`):

| API | What it does |
| :--- | :--- |
| `PantrixFont(resource, weight, style, variationSettings)` | A font: the file in the resources, and the weight and style the family registers it at. `variationSettings` is its place on a variable font's axes; if it is not given, it is what the weight and the style say. Reading ahead asks with the same settings |
| `PantrixTypeface(vararg fonts)` | A typeface, with its font files. `PantrixTypeface.Default` is the library's own typeface |
| `rememberPantrixTypography(typeface)` | Pantrix's scale, in that typeface. While the typeface changes it stays with the old one, and changes once when the new one arrives |
| `rememberPantrixFontFamily(typeface)` | Only the family (`FontFamily`) |
| `areTypefacesLoaded(vararg typefaces)` | Whether all the fonts of the typefaces given have been read. Asking starts the reading |
| `isPantrixTypefaceLoaded()` | The same, for the library's own typeface |
| `PantrixTypefaceGate(loaded, timeoutMillis, onShown, content)` | Draws the content after the typeface has been read; waits at most `timeoutMillis` |

On Android, iOS and the desktop they all answer at once: the same code is written on every platform, and it waits only on the web.

### 3.1. Say the Typeface Once

```kotlin
// commonMain
val Brand = PantrixTypeface(
    PantrixFont(Res.font.brand_regular),
    PantrixFont(Res.font.brand_medium, FontWeight.Medium),
    PantrixFont(Res.font.brand_bold, FontWeight.Bold)
)

@Composable
fun App() {
    PantrixTheme(typography = rememberPantrixTypography(Brand)) {
        // …
    }
}
```

The fonts are counted in one place; the family, and whether they have been read in the browser, are both asked of that list. If the two are counted in separate places, one day they will not match (see section 5, "The same key").

An app that uses only the library's own typeface need not say anything: `PantrixTheme { … }` is enough.

### 3.2. The Web Entry

```kotlin
// webMain
@OptIn(ExperimentalComposeUiApi::class)
fun main() {
    // On a page without the box (an old index.html the browser kept), it is set up in the body.
    val box = "app".takeIf { document.getElementById(it) != null }
    ComposeViewport(viewportContainerId = box) {
        PantrixTypefaceGate(
            loaded = areTypefacesLoaded(Brand),
            onShown = { document.getElementById("loading")?.remove() }
        ) {
            App()
        }
    }
}
```

For the library's own typeface `loaded` is not given: `PantrixTypefaceGate(onShown = …) { App() }`.

### 3.3. The Page

```html
<head>
    <!-- The typeface is downloaded while the app's code downloads. Without `crossorigin` the browser does not
         count this download as the app's own request, and the file comes down twice. -->
    <link rel="preload" as="fetch" type="font/ttf" crossorigin
          href="composeResources/<package>.generated.resources/font/brand_regular.ttf">
</head>
<body>
    <!-- The loading mark: it stands over the app until the app's first frame is drawn. -->
    <div id="loading">…</div>
    <!-- The box the app is set up in. -->
    <div id="app"></div>
    <script type="application/javascript" src="webApp.js"></script>
</body>
```

```css
html, body { width: 100%; height: 100%; margin: 0; padding: 0; overflow: hidden; }

#app { width: 100%; height: 100%; }

#loading {
    position: fixed;
    inset: 0;
    z-index: 1;
    display: flex;
    align-items: center;
    justify-content: center;
    pointer-events: none;
}
```

The `<package>` in the address is the package of the generated `Res` class of the module that carries the resources. The address of the library's own typeface is `composeResources/com.pantrixui.foundation.generated.resources/font/plus_jakarta_sans.ttf`. To be sure, build the bundle once and look in the `build/dist/…/composeResources` folder.

### 3.4. A Typeface That Changes While the App Runs

`rememberPantrixTypography(typeface)` solves this itself: when `typeface` changes, it goes on giving the old typography until the new one has been read, and gives the new one once, when all of it has arrived.

```kotlin
val typeface = if (settings.brand) Brand else PantrixTypeface.Default
PantrixTheme(typography = rememberPantrixTypography(typeface)) { /* … */ }
```

Between the choice and the change, as much time passes as the files take to download. If that too is not wanted, the typefaces are read ahead: they are all given to the gate together, and the page downloads them all ahead. The sample app in this repository does so, because it has a page that shows three typefaces side by side:

```kotlin
PantrixTypefaceGate(loaded = areTypefacesLoaded(PantrixTypeface.Default, PlusJakartaSans, Poppins)) { App() }
```

The price is the bytes downloaded: in the sample app fifteen files, 2.0 MB. For a product the right thing is mostly to read ahead only the first screen's typeface, and to leave the others to the change.

### 3.5. Characters the Fonts Lack

In a browser, Compose draws a character none of the app's fonts has (an arrow, `⌘`, an Arabic letter) in a Noto font it fetches from Google's servers (`NotoFontDownloader`, `https://fonts.gstatic.com/s/`). That has three costs:

*   Every visitor's browser asks Google for it.
*   A page that is offline leaves the character blank.
*   A content security policy (CSP) must put `https://fonts.gstatic.com` in its `connect-src`.

Compose has no general setting that turns it off. But it installs what it fetched in a public way, `FontFamily.Resolver.preload`; where a font that has the character was installed that way before, Compose sees no missing character and fetches nothing.

A `PantrixTypeface`'s `fallbacks` are those fonts. They are read with the typeface's fonts and installed in the resolver, and `areTypefacesLoaded` (the gate too) waits for them as well. The library's own typeface, `PantrixTypeface.Default`, carries Pantrix Symbols for the marks a shortcut is written in on Apple's systems and Plus Jakarta Sans lacks: `⌘ ⇧ ⌥ ⌫ ⌦ ⇥ ⇞ ⇟ ⎋`, 3 KB cut from three of Noto's fonts. An app that gives its own typeface adds it itself; an app that writes Arabic gives its own Arabic font too:

```kotlin
val Brand = PantrixTypeface(
    fonts = listOf(PantrixFont(Res.font.brand_regular), PantrixFont(Res.font.brand_bold, FontWeight.Bold)),
    fallbacks = PantrixTypeface.Default.fallbacks + PantrixFont(Res.font.noto_sans_arabic)
)
```

On Android, iOS and the desktop the system's fonts draw such a character; the fallbacks are not read there. Which characters are fetched shows, while the page is open, in `performance.getEntriesByType('resource')` as `fonts.gstatic.com` addresses.

## 4. Without Pantrix

The same solution, with Compose Multiplatform's own API only. The code below can be copied into any project; it is a simplified form of its counterparts in the library.

### 4.1. Common Code (`commonMain`)

```kotlin
/** A font: the file in the resources, and the weight and style the family registers it at. */
data class AppFont(
    val resource: FontResource,
    val weight: FontWeight = FontWeight.Normal,
    val style: FontStyle = FontStyle.Normal
)

/** The fonts' family. In the browser, a font that has not arrived yet is the fallback typeface in the family. */
@Composable
fun rememberFontFamily(fonts: List<AppFont>): FontFamily {
    val read = key(fonts) { fonts.map { Font(it.resource, it.weight, it.style) } }
    return remember(read) { FontFamily(read) }
}

/** Whether the fonts have all been read. Asking starts the reading; outside the web it is always true. */
@Composable
expect fun areFontsLoaded(fonts: List<AppFont>): Boolean

/** [value] itself if it has been read; if not, the last one read. If none has been read, [value] still. */
@Composable
fun <T> lastLoaded(value: T, loaded: Boolean): T {
    var last by remember { mutableStateOf<T?>(null) }
    if (!loaded) return last ?: value
    SideEffect { last = value }
    return value
}

/** Draws [content] after the typeface has been read; waits at most [timeoutMillis]. */
@Composable
fun FontGate(
    loaded: Boolean,
    timeoutMillis: Long = 3000,
    onShown: () -> Unit = {},
    content: @Composable () -> Unit
) {
    var waiting by remember { mutableStateOf(true) }
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
        delay(timeoutMillis)
        waiting = false
    }
    // A gate once opened stays open: an app that has been drawn is not set up again.
    var opened by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
    if (opened || loaded || !waiting) {
        SideEffect { opened = true }
        content()
        val shown by rememberUpdatedState(onShown)
        LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
            // The first frame after the frame that carries the content: that frame has been drawn.
            withFrameNanos { }
            shown()
        }
    }
}
```

### 4.2. Platform Counterparts

```kotlin
// webMain
@OptIn(ExperimentalResourceApi::class)
@Composable
actual fun areFontsLoaded(fonts: List<AppFont>): Boolean {
    // All are asked for first, then looked at: the fonts are read side by side, not one after another.
    val read = key(fonts) { fonts.map { preloadFont(it.resource, it.weight, it.style).value } }
    return read.none { it == null }
}
```

```kotlin
// androidMain, iosMain, jvmMain
@Composable
actual fun areFontsLoaded(fonts: List<AppFont>): Boolean = true
```

`preloadFont` exists only in the web source sets and carries `@ExperimentalResourceApi`; it cannot be called from common code. That is why `expect`/`actual` is needed. `webMain` is the source set Kotlin sets up by itself when the `js` and `wasmJs` targets are both defined.

### 4.3. Use

```kotlin
// commonMain
val Brand = listOf(
    AppFont(Res.font.brand_regular),
    AppFont(Res.font.brand_bold, FontWeight.Bold)
)

@Composable
fun App() {
    val family = rememberFontFamily(Brand)
    // For a typeface that changes while the app runs: it stays with the old one until the new one has been read.
    val shown = lastLoaded(family, loaded = areFontsLoaded(Brand))
    // typographyIn: your own function that sets up your typography in the family given.
    MaterialTheme(typography = typographyIn(shown)) { /* … */ }
}
```

```kotlin
// webMain
@OptIn(ExperimentalComposeUiApi::class)
fun main() {
    val box = "app".takeIf { document.getElementById(it) != null }
    ComposeViewport(viewportContainerId = box) {
        FontGate(
            loaded = areFontsLoaded(Brand),
            onShown = { document.getElementById("loading")?.remove() }
        ) {
            App()
        }
    }
}
```

The page and the style are the same as those in 3.3.

### 4.4. Characters the Fonts Lack

A fallback font is installed in the window's font resolver once it is read; it is the way Compose installs what it fetches itself:

```kotlin
// webMain
@OptIn(ExperimentalResourceApi::class)
@Composable
fun installFallbacks(fallbacks: List<FontResource>): Boolean {
    val read = fallbacks.map { preloadFont(it).value }
    val resolver = LocalFontFamilyResolver.current
    var installed by remember(fallbacks, resolver) { mutableStateOf(false) }
    LaunchedEffect(read, resolver) {
        val fonts = read.filterNotNull()
        if (fonts.size == fallbacks.size) {
            fonts.forEach { resolver.preload(FontFamily(it)) }
            installed = true
        }
    }
    return fallbacks.isEmpty() || installed
}
```

It is given to the gate with the fonts: `FontGate(loaded = areFontsLoaded(Brand) && installFallbacks(Symbols))`. The `&&` here does not hold the second call back, as both are called at every composition and the read starts at the first call; taking each into a value and joining them after is clearer.

## 5. Pitfalls

| Pitfall | What happens | What is done |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **The same key** | If the font read ahead and the font the theme asks for are not the same file **with the same weight and the same style**, it is not found in the cache; the app is drawn with the fallback again | Count the fonts in one list; set up both the family and the question from that list |
| **Asking with `&&`** | `areLoaded(a) && areLoaded(b)`: the second is not asked at all until the first arrives; the files come down one after the other | Give them all in one call |
| **A preload without `crossorigin`** | The browser does not count what it downloaded as the app's `fetch` request; the file comes down twice and a warning falls into the console | `as="fetch"` and `crossorigin` together |
| **An app set up in the body** | `ComposeViewport` clears the inside of the box it is set up in: the loading mark goes before the app's first frame, and an empty page is left between | Set up the app in its own box; remove the mark after the first frame |
| **A gate with no timeout** | If the file does not arrive (a wrong address, a broken network), the page stays empty for ever | Wait a while, then draw with the fallback |
| **A gate that can close** | If the answer turns back to "not read" later, the app is removed and loses all its state | Let a gate once opened stay open |
| **An old `index.html`** | If the browser kept the old page, there is no box; an app that looks for the box never opens | If there is no box, set up in the body |
| **Addresses written by hand** | When the module's or the file's name changes, the preload downloads for nothing; nothing breaks, the file only comes down late | A test that compares the addresses with the font folders (ours is `WebFontPreloadTest`) |
| **A hidden tab** | The browser gives no frames to a hidden tab; the app is not set up until the tab is visible | It is not a bug; while measuring, see that the tab is visible |
| **Browser tests** | Karma does not serve the resources: in tests the font never arrives, and the question always says "not read" | Give the test your own reader (`LocalResourceReader`) |
| **Reading everything ahead** | Typefaces that will never be used come down to every visitor too | Read ahead only the first screen's typeface; leave the others to the change |
| **An array in `webMain`** | In the source set that `js` and `wasmJs` share, the editor cannot resolve an array's extension: `flatMap` on a `vararg` parameter gives the warning "Cannot access 'kotlin.Cloneable' which is a supertype of 'Array'". The build passes; the warning is only in the editor | Turn the `vararg` into a list in common code; let the platform counterpart take a list (like `areFontsLoaded` in 4.1) |
| **No monospace typeface given** | `FontFamily.Monospace` resolves to no typeface in a browser (Compose on the web reaches no system font): `typography.code`, code blocks and the JSON view are drawn in a proportional fallback, and columns do not line up | Put a monospace typeface in the resources and give it with `rememberPantrixTypography(typeface, codeTypeface = …)`; read it ahead too |
| **A character the font lacks** | Compose fetches a Noto font from Google for it; offline the character stays blank, and a CSP must let Google in | Give a font that has the character as a fallback (3.5): `PantrixTypeface.Default.fallbacks` carries the marks of a Mac's keys |

## 6. Verification

### The Measuring Script

In the browser, exactly when a frame is drawn cannot be seen from outside; the order of the events can. A small script, loaded in `index.html` before the app's script, is added to a copy of the production bundle:

```js
(function () {
  const log = (m) => console.log('[font-probe] ' + Math.round(performance.now()) + 'ms ' + m);
  const isFont = (s) => s.indexOf('/font/') >= 0;
  const origFetch = window.fetch;
  window.fetch = function (u) {
    const s = String((u && u.url) || u);
    if (isFont(s)) log('fetch ' + s.split('/').pop());
    return origFetch.apply(this, arguments);
  };
  // Frames that last longer than a frame: a page set up from the start shows here.
  let last = performance.now();
  const tick = (now) => {
    if (now - last > 24) log('long frame ' + Math.round(now - last) + 'ms');
    last = now;
    if (now < 6000) requestAnimationFrame(tick);
  };
  requestAnimationFrame(tick);
})();
```

The order expected: the fonts have been read **before** the app's first long frame, and after that frame no new request for a font is seen. `performance.getEntriesByType('resource')` tells who asked for the file: if the preload works, `initiatorType` is `"link"` and the file comes down once.

### Tests

| Test | What it looks at |
| :--- | :--- |
| `ui/foundation`, `PantrixTypefaceWebTest` (in the browser) | A typeface has been read when all its fonts have been read; those asked for together are read together; what has been read is ready at the next first setup; the scale stays with the old typeface until the new one arrives |
| `ui/foundation`, `PantrixTypefaceTest` | Outside the web a typeface has been read from the start; one on its way is not given, the last one read is given |
| `ui/foundation`, `PantrixTypefaceGateTest` | The gate opens when the typeface arrives, stays open once opened, tells after the content has been drawn on the page, and gives up waiting after a while |
| `app/shared`, `WebFontPreloadTest` | The files the page downloads ahead are the same as the files in the font folders; every line carries `as="fetch"` and `crossorigin` |
| `ui/foundation`, `PantrixTypefaceWebTest` (in a browser), fallbacks | Fallbacks are asked for with the fonts; a typeface is read once its fallback is read and installed; a fallback that cannot be read keeps it waiting; a fallback that is no font breaks nothing |
| `ui/foundation`, `PantrixSymbolsOnTheDesktopTest` | Every character a shortcut is written in on Apple's systems is in Plus Jakarta Sans or in Pantrix Symbols |

## 7. Where It Is in This Repository

| File | What |
| :--- | :--- |
| `ui/foundation/src/commonMain/kotlin/com/pantrixui/foundation/token/typography/PantrixTypeface.kt` | `PantrixFont`, `PantrixTypeface`, `rememberPantrixFontFamily`, `areTypefacesLoaded`, `isPantrixTypefaceLoaded` |
| `ui/foundation/src/webMain/…/PantrixTypeface.web.kt` | The browser's part of `areTypefacesLoaded`: `areFontsLoaded` (`preloadFont`). The typefaces' fonts are gathered into one list in common code; this part only takes the list |

## 8. What Is Left Open

The items seen in this work and not touched are in `docs/OPEN_ITEMS.md`. The chief ones:

*   The library's typeface is one file, but in the browser it is read seven times; in an app that does not wait for the typeface, the weights arrive one by one.
*   `preloadFont` is experimental (`@ExperimentalResourceApi`); it can change in a later version of Compose Multiplatform.
*   It was seen only in the built-in browser and on the Wasm target; it was not looked at in real browsers or on a slow network.
*   The loading mark stalls while the Wasm compiles, and opens on a white ground on a device with a dark theme too.

# Window Title Guide

This document explains why, in Compose Multiplatform, the window of an app of one window and many screens keeps one name whatever is shown, what the library gives for it, and how it is tested. The problem is not Pantrix's own: it shows the same way in **every** Compose Multiplatform app that runs on the web and on the desktop. Section 3 of this document gives the solution with Pantrix's API, and section 4 without the library, in a form any project can copy.

What is said here of Compose was read in the sources of Compose Multiplatform 1.12.2 (`Window.desktop.kt`, `ComponentUpdater.kt`, `LocalAwtWindow.kt`, `ComposeWindowPanel.desktop.kt`). What could not be verified is counted in section 7.

## 1. The Problem

### Symptom

*   On the web every page of the app has the same name on the browser's tab: the `<title>` of `index.html`. A user with ten tabs open cannot see which one is "Orders"; every entry of the browser's history has the same name too.
*   On the desktop the window's title bar, the taskbar and the window switcher show the name given to `Window(title = …)`, whatever screen the app is on.
*   The screen's name is known already, and written in its bar; but there is no common API that carries it to the window.

### Cause

A window's title is not in common code. On each platform it is a field of another object:

| Platform | The window's title | From common code |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Web (`js`, `wasmJs`) | `document.title`: the name of the tab and of the history | None; `kotlinx.browser.document` is in the web source set alone |
| Desktop (JVM) | `java.awt.Frame.title`: the title bar, the taskbar | None; the window is reached through `LocalAwtWindow`, which is `@ExperimentalComposeUiApi` |
| Android | No window's title a user sees: the recent apps say the app's name | No need |
| iOS | No window's title a user sees: the app switcher says the app's name | No need |

Two details make it harder:

1.  **More than one screen is there at once.** While one page slides over another both are in the composition; in a wide window a list and its detail stand side by side. "Write the title as a screen opens and put the old one back as it closes" is not enough: the second screen opens, the first one puts the very first title back as it closes, and the open screen's name is lost.
2.  **On the desktop `Window` writes a title too.** `Window(title = …)` writes its title again only when its own value changes (`ComponentUpdater` compares it with the one before); as long as it does not, the title a screen gave stays, and when it does, it is written over it.

## 2. The Solution

A stack of titles is kept for each window. A screen that comes into the composition puts its title at the end of the stack, and one that leaves takes its own title out of it. The window is given the name at the end of the stack; once the stack is empty, the window's own title, read before the first screen came, is put back. Where a screen's title changes, the window changes with it while that screen is at the end of the stack. The app's name is added by a format: a function from the screen's name to the window's, given once at the app's root.

## 3. With Pantrix

```kotlin
import com.pantrixui.foundation.platform.LocalPantrixWindowTitleFormat
import com.pantrixui.foundation.platform.PantrixWindowTitle
import com.pantrixui.foundation.platform.PantrixWindowTitleFormat

// At the app's root, once: the app's name after each screen's.
CompositionLocalProvider(LocalPantrixWindowTitleFormat provides PantrixWindowTitleFormat { "$it · Admin" }) {
    App()
}

// In a screen: while it is shown, the window is called "Orders · Admin".
@Composable
fun OrdersScreen() {
    PantrixWindowTitle("Orders")
    OrdersList()
}
```

*   `PantrixWindowTitle(title)`: gives the window the screen's name for as long as the screen is in the composition. It writes `document.title` on the web and the window's title on the desktop; on Android and iOS it does nothing.
*   `LocalPantrixWindowTitleFormat`: how the screen's name is written as the window's. Unless given, `PantrixWindowTitleFormat.Plain`: the name as it is.
*   `PantrixPageScaffold` does it itself: each page gives the window its own `title`. An app that builds its screens with it does not call `PantrixWindowTitle` besides.

### 3.1. Pages Inside Pages

A page inside another page's content, as a preview of a page or an example of one is, gives the window no name: it leaves the title to the page it stands in. Two pages side by side, a list and its detail, are not one inside the other; both give a name, and the one that came last wins.

## 4. Without Pantrix

### 4.1. Common Code (`commonMain`)

```kotlin
/** A window's titles: the last one given first. */
class WindowTitles(private val read: () -> String, private val write: (String) -> Unit) {
    private val given = mutableListOf<Entry>()
    private var own: String? = null

    inner class Entry(title: String) {
        var title: String = title
            set(value) {
                if (field == value) return
                field = value
                if (given.lastOrNull() === this) write(value)
            }

        fun add() {
            if (given.isEmpty()) own = read()
            given.remove(this)
            given += this
            write(title)
        }

        fun remove() {
            val wasLast = given.lastOrNull() === this
            if (!given.remove(this) || !wasLast) return
            val before = given.lastOrNull()
            if (before != null) write(before.title) else own?.let(write).also { own = null }
        }
    }
}

@Composable
expect fun windowTitles(): WindowTitles?

@Composable
fun WindowTitle(title: String) {
    val titles = windowTitles() ?: return
    val entry = remember(titles) { titles.Entry(title) }
    DisposableEffect(entry) {
        entry.add()
        onDispose { entry.remove() }
    }
    SideEffect { entry.title = title }
}
```

### 4.2. The Platforms' Counterparts

```kotlin
// webMain: the page has one title.
private val documentTitles = WindowTitles(read = { document.title }, write = { document.title = it })

@Composable
actual fun windowTitles(): WindowTitles? = documentTitles
```

```kotlin
// jvmMain: each window's own titles, which go with the window once it is let go.
private val frameTitles = WeakHashMap<Frame, WindowTitles>()

@OptIn(ExperimentalComposeUiApi::class)
@Composable
actual fun windowTitles(): WindowTitles? {
    val frame = LocalAwtWindow.current as? Frame ?: return null
    return remember(frame) {
        synchronized(frameTitles) {
            frameTitles.getOrPut(frame) { WindowTitles(read = { frame.title.orEmpty() }, write = { frame.title = it }) }
        }
    }
}
```

```kotlin
// androidMain and iosMain: no window's title a user sees.
@Composable
actual fun windowTitles(): WindowTitles? = null
```

## 5. Testing

The stack's rules have no platform and are tested on every target: the last name given wins, a name that leaves makes way for the one before it, the window's own title comes back once the last name is gone, and a name that is not at the end changes nothing of the window.

```kotlin
val titles = WindowTitles(read = { window }, write = { window = it })
val orders = titles.Entry("Orders")
val order = titles.Entry("Order 42")
orders.add()
order.add()
assertEquals("Order 42", window)
order.remove()
assertEquals("Orders", window)
```

On the web `document.title` is read in a real browser: a screen writes it in its format, changes it as its title changes, and puts the page's own `<title>` back as it leaves the composition. The desktop's tests open no window (`LocalAwtWindow` is `null` in a test): there `PantrixWindowTitle` does nothing; the page's JVM tests call it so.

## 6. Pitfalls

*   **The first frame.** On the web the tab shows the `<title>` of `index.html` until the app has drawn its first frame; the screen's name comes after the first composition. The page's `<title>` is to stay the app's name.
*   **If `Window(title = …)` changes.** On the desktop Compose writes the title given to `Window` when it changes, and the screen's name is gone; it stays so until a screen comes into the composition again. The app's own name is to be given as a title that does not change.
*   **Dialogs.** A screen inside a `DialogWindow` gives the main window no name: `LocalAwtWindow` is the dialog itself there, which is no `Frame`.

## 7. Verification

### Tests

| What | Where | Target |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| The stack's rules | `ui/foundation/src/commonTest/…/platform/WindowTitlesTest.kt` | JVM, iOS, JS, Wasm |
| The browser's tab | `ui/foundation/src/webTest/…/platform/WindowTitleOnTheWebTest.kt` | JS, Wasm |
| A page naming the tab, and a page inside it not | `ui/components/src/webTest/…/PageScaffoldOnTheWebTest.kt` | JS, Wasm |

### Behaviours Broken by Hand

With the web's counterpart giving `null`, both browser tests turned red; with a page naming the window whether or not it stands inside another, the page's browser test turned red.

### Not Verified

*   The name of a scene in iPadOS's multitasking views: this library writes nothing on iOS.
*   The names of the entries of the browser's history.

## 8. Where It Is in This Repository

*   The API: `ui/foundation/src/commonMain/kotlin/com/pantrixui/foundation/platform/PantrixWindowTitle.kt`, with the platforms' counterparts in the same package's `webMain`, `jvmMain`, `androidMain` and `iosMain` files.
*   What uses it: `ui/components/src/commonMain/kotlin/com/pantrixui/components/container/page/PageFrame.kt`.
*   The demo: the app's theme gives the format (`app/shared/…/theme/Theme.kt`); the "The window's title" example of the "Page Scaffold" page (`app/shared/…/samples/PageScaffoldSamples.kt`).

What components say or announce themselves, in one language. `forLocale` picks the pack for a locale, and English stands in for a language without one.

Every field's default is its English. An app's own pack names the fields it has words for, `PantrixStrings(loading = "Laden", close = "Schließen")`, and goes on compiling when a new component brings a new field: that one is said in English until the pack has words for it, which is heard and can be mended, where a build that broke could not ship.

- `loading: String`: What a spinner, a skeleton and a loading button are announced as.

Members:

- `fun number(value: Int): String`: `value` in this language's digits: `12` as `12`, and as `١٢` where the digits are Arabic's. A sign before the number is kept as it is. What a component writes a number with where it shows one: a page's number, a count.
- `fun decimal(value: Number, fractionDigits: Int = 2, minFractionDigits: Int = 0, grouped: Boolean = true): String`: `value` as a quantity is written in this language: `1234.5` as `1,234.5`, as `1.234,5` in Turkish and as `١٬٢٣٤٫٥` in Arabic. What a chart writes beside its axis, and what any screen writes an amount or a measure with. A number that only counts or names, a page's or a year's, is `number`'s, which puts no mark between its digits.

  It is rounded to `fractionDigits` after the mark, a half away from nought, and the noughts that end a fraction are left out down to `minFractionDigits`: `2.50` is `2.5`, and `2.50` with two of both. A Double holds fifteen digits to be trusted, and what is asked for past them is not written.

  The same on every platform: it is worked out here, and asks no platform for its own format.

  `grouped`: whether each three digits of the whole are set apart by `groupSeparator`.
- `fun compact(value: Number, fractionDigits: Int = 1): String`: `value` written short, by the thousand: `1234` as `1.2K`, `2500000` as `2.5M`, and in Turkish as `1,2 B` and `2,5 Mn`. What stands where there is no room for every digit: beside a chart's axis, in a badge, on a card. Below a thousand it is `decimal`'s.

  It is rounded to `fractionDigits` after the mark and written without the noughts that end a fraction; a number that rounds up to a thousand of its kind is one of the next, `999950` being `1M` and not `1000K`.
- `fun percent(share: Number, fractionDigits: Int = 0): String`: `share` of a whole as a share of a hundred: `0.256` as `26%`, as `%26` in Turkish, and `1.0` as `100%`. `fractionDigits` are those of the number before the sign: `0.256` with one is `25.6%`.
- `fun characterCount(count: Int, max: Int): String`: `Characters entered: {count} of {max}` as `Characters entered: 12 of 40`: what a screen reader says for a text field's counter, which shows digits alone.

  It is worded so that no language needs the number to agree with the noun, which a template cannot do.

  `count`: how many characters the field holds.

  `max`: how many characters it may hold.
- `fun remove(label: String): String`: `Remove {label}` as `Remove Kotlin`: what a screen reader says for the button that takes `label` out, so that a row of such buttons can be told apart.

  The name goes in as it is written, with no ending added to it, which a template could not get right in a language that inflects.
- `fun slidePosition(position: Int, count: Int): String`: `Slide {position} of {count}` as `Slide 2 of 5`: what a screen reader says for where a carousel is, which shows dots alone. `position` counts from one.

  It is worded so that no language needs the number to agree with the noun, which a template cannot do.

  `count`: how many slides the carousel has.
- `fun itemCount(count: Int): String`: `Items: {count}` as `Items: 3`: what a screen reader says for how many things a folded object or array of a JSON view holds, which shows the number alone.

  It is worded so that no language needs the number to agree with the noun, which a template cannot do.

  `count`: how many items the folded object or array holds.
- `fun findingCount(count: Int): String`: `Findings: {count}` as `Findings: 3`: what a screen reader says for the button of a diagnostics inspector, which shows the number alone. Worded, as `itemCount` is, so that no language needs the number to agree with a noun.

  `count`: how many findings the inspector holds.
- `fun overLimit(count: Int): String`: `{count} over the limit` as `12 over the limit`: what a text area's counter says, and a screen reader is told, once its text is past its limit. Worded, as `itemCount` is, so that no language needs the number to agree with a noun.

  `count`: how many characters the text is past its limit.
- `fun jsonUnreadable(line: Int, column: Int): String`: `JSON could not be read: line {line}, column {column}` as `JSON could not be read: line 3, column 14`: what a JSON view says over a text it could not read, with the place it stopped at. Both count from one.

  `line`: the line the reading stopped at.

  `column`: the column the reading stopped at.
- `fun level(level: Int): String`: `Level {level}` as `Level 2`: what a screen reader says for how deep a part of a tree is, which the eye is told by an indent. `level` counts from one: the outermost part is at the first level.
- `fun page(page: Int): String`: `Page {page}` as `Page 4`: what a screen reader says for a page's button in a pagination, which shows the number alone. `page` counts from one.
- `fun pageOf(page: Int, count: Int): String`: `Page {page} of {count}` as `Page 3 of 10`: where a pagination is, written between its two buttons where the row is too narrow for the pages' numbers. `page` counts from one.

  It is worded so that no language needs the number to agree with the noun, which a template cannot do.

  `count`: how many pages there are.
- `fun sortOrder(position: Int): String`: `Sort order {position}` as `Sort order 2`: what a screen reader says for a column's place among the columns a table is in the order of, which the header shows as a number alone. `position` counts from one.
- `fun selectRow(label: String?): String`: `Select {label}` as `Select Order 4801`: what a screen reader says for the box that chooses the row named `label`, so that a column of such boxes can be told apart. A row without a name is `selectRow` alone.

  `count`: how many rows the table has in all.

  It is worded so that no language needs the number to agree with the noun, which a template cannot do.

  `count`: how many rows are chosen.
- `fun columnWidth(label: String): String`: `Width of {label}` as `Width of City`: what a screen reader says for the end of the header of the column named `label`, where the column's width is changed. The width itself is said after it, as a number.
- `fun flowFrom(label: String): String`: `From {label}` as `From Visits`: what a sankey calls a flow that comes into a node from the node named `label`.
- `fun flowTo(label: String): String`: `To {label}` as `To Sign-ups`: what a sankey calls a flow that goes out of a node to the node named `label`.
- `fun shareOfFirst(share: String): String`: `{label} of the first` as `41.3% of the first`: a stage of a funnel as `share`, written, of the first stage.
- `fun shareOfPrevious(share: String): String`: `{label} of the previous` as `52.1% of the previous`: a stage of a funnel as `share` of the stage before it.
- `fun more(count: Int): String`: `+{count} more` as `+3 more`: what a list says in the place of the `count` rows it has no room for, as a chart's tooltip does under those it shows.

  It is worded so that no language needs the number to agree with the noun, which a template cannot do.
- `fun dateFormat(pattern: String): String`: `Enter the date as {pattern}` as `Enter the date as MM/DD/YYYY`: a date field's error for a date not whole.

  `pattern`: the order the field takes a date in, as this language writes it: `MM/DD/YYYY`.
- `fun dateBetween(start: String, end: String): String`: `Choose a day from {start} to {end}` as `Choose a day from Oct 1, 2026 to Oct 31, 2026`: a date field's error for a day outside `start` and `end`, both written.
- `fun dateFrom(start: String): String`: `Choose {start} or a later day`: a date field's error for a day before `start`, written, which has no last.
- `fun dateUntil(end: String): String`: `Choose {end} or an earlier day`: a date field's error for a day after `end`, written, which has no first.
- `fun timeFormat(pattern: String): String`: `Enter the time as {pattern}` as `Enter the time as HH:MM`: a time field's error for a time not whole.

  `pattern`: how the field takes a time, as this language writes it: `HH:MM`.
- `fun timeBetween(start: String, end: String): String`: `Choose a time from {start} to {end}` as `Choose a time from 09:00 to 18:00`: a time field's error for a time outside `start` and `end`, both written.
- `fun timeFrom(start: String): String`: `Choose {start} or a later time`: a time field's error for a time before `start`, written, which has no last.
- `fun timeUntil(end: String): String`: `Choose {end} or an earlier time`: a time field's error for a time after `end`, written, which has no first.
- `fun filesAdded(count: Int): String`: `Files added: {count}` as `Files added: 2`: how many files a drop zone took, told to a screen reader.

  `count`: how many files the drop zone took.
- `fun filesRejected(count: Int): String`: `Files not accepted: {count}` as `Files not accepted: 1`: how many it did not take.

  `count`: how many files it did not take.
- `fun fileSize(bytes: Long): String`: `bytes` as a file's size: `512 B`, `1.2 KB`, `34 MB`, and `1,2 KB` in Turkish. A size is counted by the thousand, as Android's and Apple's systems count it, and written with one digit after the mark under ten of its kind and none from ten on; one that rounds up to a thousand of its kind is one of the next, `999999` being `1 MB`. Sizes past the gigabytes are written in gigabytes.
- `fun range(first: String, last: String): String`: `{first} to {last}` as `Mar to Jul`: a stretch from the thing named `first` to the one named `last`, as the part of a chart that is in view is said.
- `fun month(month: Int): String`: The short name of the month `month` of a year, counted from one for January: `Oct` for ten. A month before the first is taken for January and one past the twelfth for December.
- `fun dayMonth(day: Int, month: Int): String`: A day of a year without its year, in this language's order and digits: `Oct 13`, and `13 Eki` in Turkish.

  `day`: the day of the month, from 1.

  `month`: the month, from 1 for January.
- `fun monthYear(month: Int, year: Int): String`: A month of a year: `Oct 2026`.

  `month`: the month, from 1 for January.

  `year`: the year.
- `fun date(day: Int, month: Int, year: Int): String`: A day: `Oct 13, 2026`, and `13 Eki 2026` in Turkish.

  `day`: the day of the month, from 1.

  `month`: the month, from 1 for January.

  `year`: the year.
- `fun clock(hour: Int, minute: Int, second: Int? = null): String`: A time of day by a clock of twenty-four hours, each part in two digits of this language's: `09:05`, and `09:05:07` where `second` is given.

  `hour`: the hour, from 0 to 23.

  `minute`: the minute, from 0 to 59.
- `fun time(hour: Int, minute: Int, second: Int? = null, is24Hour: Boolean): String`: A time of day in this language's digits, the hour `hour` counted by a clock of twenty-four: by twenty-four hours where `is24Hour`, as `clock` writes it, `22:05`; by twelve where not, the hour in no more digits than it has and the half of the day after it or before it as `twelveHourTemplate` puts it, `10:05 PM`, and `ÖS 10:05` in Turkish. Which clock is the caller's to say: a time picker's `is24Hour`.

  `minute`: the minute, from 0 to 59.

  `second`: the second, from 0 to 59, written after the minute where it is given.
- `fun longMonth(month: Int): String`: The full name of the month `month` of a year, counted from one for January: `October` for ten. A month before the first is taken for January and one past the twelfth for December, as `month` takes them.
- `fun weekday(dayOfWeek: Int): String`: The full name of the day of the week `dayOfWeek`, as ISO 8601 numbers the days: `Monday` for one and `Sunday` for seven. The days go round as the weeks do: eight is a Monday again, and nought a Sunday.
- `fun shortWeekday(dayOfWeek: Int): String`: The short name a calendar writes over the column of the day of the week `dayOfWeek`: `Mo` for one.
- `fun longMonthYear(month: Int, year: Int): String`: A month of a year by the month's full name: `October 2026`, a calendar's title.

  `month`: the month, from 1 for January.

  `year`: the year.
- `fun longDate(day: Int, month: Int, year: Int): String`: A day said in full, with the day of the week it falls on: `Saturday, October 17, 2026`, and `17 Ekim 2026 Cumartesi` in Turkish. What a screen reader hears a calendar's day as.

  `day`: the day of the month, from 1.

  `month`: the month, from 1 for January.

  `year`: the year.

On the type:

- `PantrixStrings.forLocale(locale: PantrixLocale): PantrixStrings`: Falls back to English for any language without a pack.

  Falling back is deliberate: an untranslated screen reader announcement is recoverable, an empty one is not.

  `locale`: the locale whose language the pack is wanted for: its primary subtag alone counts.
- `PantrixStrings.Arabic: PantrixStrings`: Pantrix's words in Arabic.
- `PantrixStrings.Turkish: PantrixStrings`: Pantrix's words in Turkish.
- `PantrixStrings.English: PantrixStrings`: English: every field's own default. A pack of another language names each field, and one it leaves out is said in English.

# com.pantrixui:annotations: the API no page documents

Annotations that describe a Pantrix UI component and its examples.

## Package com.pantrixui.annotations

### PantrixComponent

`import com.pantrixui.annotations.PantrixComponent`, from `com.pantrixui:annotations`

```kotlin
annotation class PantrixComponent(
    public val name: String,
    public val category: String,
    public val description: String,
    public val keywords: Array<String>
)
```

Marks a composable as a Pantrix component and describes it for tooling.

Every component carries one, on its primary overload, with two or more `PantrixExample`s, and a new component gets them in the same change. At build time the demo catalogue counts them, detekt's `UnmarkedComponent` checks that every component carries them, and the documents for coding assistants are written from them (docs/guide/ai/AI_GUIDE.md): a component's name, group, description and keywords are what an assistant is told of it first, and its examples what it copies. They are written with the component because the description is cheapest to capture from the person who wrote it, while the reasons are still in their head: one written later says what the code does rather than what the component is for.

Binary retention, so a tool can read them from a published klib as well as from sources in the same build.

Parameters:

- `name: String`: the component's name without the `Pantrix` prefix, e.g. `Button`
- `category: String`: the package group under `com.pantrixui.components` it lives in, e.g. `elements`
- `description: String`: one sentence on what it is for, not how it is drawn
- `keywords: Array<String>`: the words someone looking for the component would use that its name does not say, so that a search finds it by them: what other design systems and platforms call it, and what it is used for, e.g. `toast` and `undo` for a snackbar. Three to eight, in English and in lower case; a keyword of more than one word has a space between them. The documents for coding assistants stop the build on a component that gives none.

### PantrixExample

`import com.pantrixui.annotations.PantrixExample`, from `com.pantrixui:annotations`

```kotlin
annotation class PantrixExample(
    public val title: String,
    public val code: String
)
```

A usage example for a `PantrixComponent`. Repeatable: a component carries two or more.

`code` is a snippet a reader could paste into a composable, not a complete file. User-facing text in it comes from resources rather than string literals, because examples are what gets copied. The compiler never reads `code`: the documents for coding assistants check, at every build, that each argument it gives by name to the library's own functions and constructors is a parameter of one of their forms, and the rest is kept in step with the component's signature by hand.

Parameters:

- `title: String`: what the example shows, in a few words
- `code: String`: the snippet

### PantrixComponentPart

`import com.pantrixui.annotations.PantrixComponentPart`, from `com.pantrixui:annotations`

```kotlin
annotation class PantrixComponentPart(
    public val of: String
)
```

Marks a public composable as a part of a component, in place of `PantrixComponent`: a variant of it, or a piece that is only used inside it, such as a menu's item or a divider drawn across.

A part has no examples of its own: its component's examples show it. detekt's `UnmarkedComponent` accepts it where it would ask for a `PantrixComponent`.

Parameters:

- `of: String`: the name of the component it belongs to, without the `Pantrix` prefix, e.g. `Menu`

# com.pantrixui:testing: the API no page documents

Test helpers for apps built on Pantrix UI: finding components by their tags, a test theme and doubles.

## Package com.pantrixui.testing

### ComposeUiTest.assertNoFindings

`import com.pantrixui.testing.assertNoFindings`, from `com.pantrixui:testing`

```kotlin
fun ComposeUiTest.assertNoFindings(findings: PantrixFindings)
```

Asserts that the theme's diagnostics found nothing on the screen: no control without a name, no words too faint to read on what they stand on, no touch target squeezed, no tag on two nodes. A squeezed touch target is reported once it has lasted half a second and a tag on two nodes once it has lasted a second and a half, so the test's clock is moved on past that first. `findings` is the sink the screen's theme was given, as `PantrixTestTheme`'s `findings`.

Parameters:

- `findings: PantrixFindings`

Presses `shortcut` on the node as a keyboard of `system` does: Command leads it on Apple's systems and Control on the others, so that one test of `PantrixShortcut(Key.K, command = true)` presses `⌘K` on a Mac and `Ctrl+K` elsewhere. The screen answers it where it is typed on `system` too: `PantrixTestTheme`'s `system`. The node takes the keys where it has the focus or holds what has it.

- `system: OperatingSystem`

### hasPantrixTag

`import com.pantrixui.testing.hasPantrixTag`, from `com.pantrixui:testing`

```kotlin
fun hasPantrixTag(
    component: String,
    tagKey: String? = null,
    scope: String? = null
): SemanticsMatcher
```

Whether a node carries the automation tag of the Pantrix component `component` given `tagKey`, inside `scope`: `hasPantrixTag("Button", "save", scope = "Checkout")` is the node tagged `Checkout.Button_save`. A test names the component and its key as the screen's code does, and the tag is built as the component builds it, so that a key written `Save draft` is found as `Button_save_draft`.

Without `tagKey`, a node of the component matches whatever its key, and so does one of a component given none: every button of the scope. Without `scope`, the tag has none, and a component inside a `TestScope` is found by naming its scope. A part of a control with a key stands inside the control's tag: the segment `newest` of a segment button keyed `sort` is `hasPantrixTag("Segment", "newest", scope = "SegmentButton_sort")`.

Parameters:

- `component: String`: the component's name, as its tag begins: `Button`, `TextField`, `Chart`.
- `tagKey: String?`: the key the component was given, as the screen's code wrote it; null for any key.
- `scope: String?`: the chain of `TestScope`s the component stands in, `Checkout.Payment`, or the tag of the control a part stands in; null outside one.

### SemanticsNodeInteractionsProvider.onPantrixNode

```kotlin
fun SemanticsNodeInteractionsProvider.onPantrixNode(
    component: String,
    tagKey: String? = null,
    scope: String? = null,
    useUnmergedTree: Boolean = false
): SemanticsNodeInteraction
```

The one node of the screen that carries the automation tag of `component` given `tagKey`, inside `scope`: see `hasPantrixTag`. What is done with it fails where there is none, or more than one.

Parameters:

- `component: String`
- `tagKey: String?`
- `scope: String?`
- `useUnmergedTree: Boolean`: whether to look in the tree of every node, rather than in the one a screen reader reads, in which a node that merges what it holds stands for all of it.

### SemanticsNodeInteractionsProvider.onAllPantrixNodes

`import com.pantrixui.testing.onAllPantrixNodes`, from `com.pantrixui:testing`

```kotlin
fun SemanticsNodeInteractionsProvider.onAllPantrixNodes(
    component: String,
```

Every node of the screen that carries the automation tag of `component` given `tagKey`, inside `scope`, in the order of the tree: see `hasPantrixTag`. Without a key, every one of the component in that scope.

Parameters:

- `tagKey: String?`
- `scope: String?`
- `useUnmergedTree: Boolean`: whether to look in the tree of every node, rather than in the one a screen reader reads, in which a node that merges what it holds stands for all of it.

### SemanticsNodeInteractionsProvider.pantrixTags

`import com.pantrixui.testing.pantrixTags`, from `com.pantrixui:testing`

```kotlin
fun SemanticsNodeInteractionsProvider.pantrixTags(useUnmergedTree: Boolean = true): List<String>
```

The Pantrix automation tags the screen carries, in the order of its tree: what a test, or a flow of the platform's UI automation such as Maestro, finds its nodes by. A tag is written as Pantrix writes one, the chain of its scopes and then a name and a key, `Checkout.Button_pay`. A component given no key takes its tag from where it is called, `Button#1k3z9`, and that tag changes when the code moves: give the component a `tagKey`. A tag of another shape, as an app's own `Modifier.testTag("login")`, is left out.

Parameters:

- `useUnmergedTree: Boolean`: whether to look in the tree of every node, as by default, rather than in the one a screen reader reads, in which a node that merges what it holds hides the tags inside it.

### PantrixTestTheme

`import com.pantrixui.testing.PantrixTestTheme`, from `com.pantrixui:testing`

```kotlin
@Composable
fun PantrixTestTheme(
    platform: PlatformType = PlatformType.Android,
    system: OperatingSystem = platform.system,
    dark: Boolean = false,
    locale: PantrixLocale = PantrixLocale.English,
    density: PantrixDensity = PantrixDensity.Comfortable,
    fontScale: Float = 1f,
    window: PantrixWindow? = null,
    findings: PantrixFindings? = null,
    analytics: PantrixAnalytics = PantrixAnalytics.NoOp,
    haptics: PantrixHaptics = PantrixHaptics.NoOp,
    clipboard: TestClipboard? = null,
    filePicker: FilePicker? = null,
    clock: TestClock? = null,
    content: @Composable () -> Unit
)
```

Pantrix's theme as a test sees a screen: the same on every machine and in every run, whatever the device under the test. By default the screen is on Android, in the light theme and in English, at the comfortable density and a font scale of one, with motion reduced so that nothing is caught moving; each is a parameter where a test needs another.

The diagnostics are on: what they find goes to `findings`, which `assertNoFindings` reads, or to the log where the test gives no sink. The platform's services are the test's own: `analytics` and `haptics` keep what the screen tells them where the test gives recorders, `clipboard` keeps what it copies, `filePicker` answers its pickers and `clock` is the time it reads. Left out, the clipboard and the picker are the theme's own, so that nothing of the machine's is written to or opened; the clock is the device's. The screen's file saver is always the theme's own, a `TestFileSaver`: a test that reads what was saved gives its own through `LocalFileSaver`, inside the theme.

```kotlin
val findings = PantrixFindings()
val analytics = RecordingAnalytics()
setContent { PantrixTestTheme(findings = findings, analytics = analytics) { CheckoutScreen() } }
onPantrixNode("Button", "pay").performClick()
assertEquals(listOf("click"), analytics.eventsOf("Button").map { it.action })
assertNoFindings(findings)
```

Parameters:

- `platform: PlatformType`: the platform the screen is shown as: its touch targets, its focus rings and its own ways.
- `system: OperatingSystem`: the operating system the screen is typed on, which says whether its shortcuts lead with Command or Control: by default the platform's own, and Windows on the desktop and the web.
- `dark: Boolean`: whether the theme is the dark one.
- `locale: PantrixLocale`: the language the screen is in, and with it the direction of its writing.
- `density: PantrixDensity`: how close together the screen's controls stand.
- `fontScale: Float`: how much larger the system writes than the theme's sizes: `2f` for Android's largest.
- `window: PantrixWindow?`: the window the screen is told it is in, its size and its folds: a phone's, a tablet's, one half of a foldable; null for the one the test draws in.
- `findings: PantrixFindings?`: where the diagnostics' findings are kept; null to write them to the log.
- `analytics: PantrixAnalytics`: what the screen's components report to.
- `haptics: PantrixHaptics`: what the screen's components play their feedback with.
- `clipboard: TestClipboard?`: the clipboard the screen copies to, with the traits it has; null for one of the theme's own.
- `filePicker: FilePicker?`: the picker the screen's pickers open, `rememberFilePicker()` and the file drop zones; null for one of the theme's own, which never answers, as a user who closes it.
- `clock: TestClock?`: the time the screen reads: its today, the hour a time picker opens at, a chart's moments; null for the device's.
- `content: @Composable () -> Unit`: the screen.

### ComposeUiTest.onEachPlatform

`import com.pantrixui.testing.onEachPlatform`, from `com.pantrixui:testing`

```kotlin
fun ComposeUiTest.onEachPlatform(
    content: @Composable (platform: PlatformType) -> Unit,
    check: ComposeUiTest.(platform: PlatformType) -> Unit
)
```

Looks at `content` on each platform in turn, in the one run of the test: `content` is composed anew for each, in the order of `PlatformType`, and `check` follows it.

One run, and not a run for each platform: on the web a run is a promise the test hands back, and a test that starts several from a loop hands back none of them, so that nothing waits for them and what fails in them fails no test.

```kotlin
onEachPlatform({ platform -> PantrixTestTheme(platform = platform) { SaveButton() } }) { platform ->
    onPantrixNode("Button", "save").assertTouchTargetOf(platform)
}
```

Parameters:

- `content: @Composable (platform: PlatformType) -> Unit`: the screen as it is shown on a platform.
- `check: ComposeUiTest.(platform: PlatformType) -> Unit`: what is asserted of it there.

### RecordingAnalytics

`import com.pantrixui.testing.RecordingAnalytics`, from `com.pantrixui:testing`

```kotlin
class RecordingAnalytics : PantrixAnalytics
```

Analytics that keep what the screen's components report, in order: what a test reads to see that a press, an open or a choice was told. `PantrixTestTheme` gives them to the screen as its `analytics`.

```kotlin
val analytics = RecordingAnalytics()
setContent { PantrixTestTheme(analytics = analytics) { CheckoutScreen() } }
onPantrixNode("Button", "pay").performClick()
assertEquals(listOf("click"), analytics.eventsOf("Button").map { it.action })
```

Members:

- `events: List<PantrixUiEvent>`: Every event reported since these were made or last cleared, in order: a copy, which later events leave alone.
- `fun eventsOf(component: String): List<PantrixUiEvent>`: The events `component` reported, in order: `eventsOf("Button")`.
- `fun clear()`: Forgets every event reported so far.

### RecordingHaptics

`import com.pantrixui.testing.RecordingHaptics`, from `com.pantrixui:testing`

```kotlin
class RecordingHaptics : PantrixHaptics
```

Haptics that keep the feedback the screen's components play, in order, and play none on the device: what a test reads to see that a long press or a choice was felt. `PantrixTestTheme` gives them to the screen as its `haptics`.

Members:

- `played: List<HapticType>`: Every feedback played since these were made or last cleared, in order: a copy, which later ones leave alone.
- `fun clear()`: Forgets every feedback played so far.

### TestClipboard

`import com.pantrixui.testing.TestClipboard`, from `com.pantrixui:testing`

```kotlin
class TestClipboard(
    public val traits: ClipboardTraits = ClipboardTraits()
) : Clipboard
```

A clipboard of the test's own, in the place of the machine's: it keeps what the screen copies, and touches nothing the machine has copied. `PantrixTestTheme` gives it to the screen as Compose's clipboard and `traits` as the platform's, so that a test sees a screen on Android 13, whose system shows a copy itself, by `ClipboardTraits(announcedBySystem = true)`, and in a page served over plain http, which has no clipboard, by `ClipboardTraits(writable = false)`.

```kotlin
val clipboard = TestClipboard()
setContent { PantrixTestTheme(clipboard = clipboard) { InviteScreen() } }
onPantrixNode("Button", "copy_link").performClick()
assertEquals("https://example.com/invite/42", clipboard.text())
```

Parameters:

- `traits: ClipboardTraits`: what the clipboard is like, as the screen is told.

Members:

- `entries: List<ClipEntry?>`: What was put on the clipboard, in order and in the platform's own type: null where it was cleared.
- `suspend fun texts(): List<String>`: The plain texts put on the clipboard, in order: what the screen copied. On the web a text is read as the browser reads it, which is waited for; an entry that holds no plain text is left out.
- `suspend fun text(): String?`: The plain text on the clipboard now, or null while it holds none.
- `fun clear()`: Forgets what was put on the clipboard.

### TestClock

`import com.pantrixui.testing.TestClock`, from `com.pantrixui:testing`

```kotlin
class TestClock(
    now: Instant,
    public val utcOffset: (Instant) -> Duration = { Duration.ZERO }
) : Clock
```

A clock of the test's own: it shows the moment the test sets, and moves only when the test moves it. `PantrixTestTheme` gives it to the screen as the screen's clock, at the offset from UTC that `utcOffset` gives: the screen reads its today, the hour a time picker opens at and a chart's moments by it.

It is the time the screen reads, and not the frames of the test: a screen that waits until midnight waits on the test's own clock as well, `mainClock.advanceTimeBy(…)`.

```kotlin
val clock = TestClock(Instant.parse("2026-10-17T21:59:00Z")) { 3.hours }
setContent { PantrixTestTheme(clock = clock) { BookingScreen() } }
clock.advanceBy(1.minutes)
mainClock.advanceTimeBy(60_000)
```

Parameters:

- `now: Instant`: the moment the clock shows at first.
- `utcOffset: (Instant) -> Duration`: how far the clock is ahead of UTC at a moment: three hours in Istanbul, less than nought west of Greenwich; by default none, the clock of UTC.

Members:

- `now: Instant`: The moment the clock shows, which the test may set.
- `fun advanceBy(duration: Duration)`: Moves the clock on by `duration`, or back where `duration` is less than nought.

### TestFilePicker

`import com.pantrixui.testing.TestFilePicker`, from `com.pantrixui:testing`

```kotlin
class TestFilePicker(
    public var files: List<PantrixFile> = emptyList()
) : FilePicker
```

A file picker of the test's own: it answers a pick with the `files` the test gives it, as a user who chooses them, and keeps what each pick asked for. It answers with the files of the kinds the pick shows and no others, and with the first of them alone where the pick takes one, as the platform's picker lets a user choose; with none of those it does not answer, as a user who closes the picker. `PantrixTestTheme` gives it to the screen in the place of the platform's.

```kotlin
val picker = TestFilePicker(listOf(PantrixFile("offer.pdf", bytes)))
setContent { PantrixTestTheme(filePicker = picker) { OfferScreen() } }
onPantrixNode("FileDrop", "offer").performClick()
assertEquals(listOf(PantrixFileType.Pdf), picker.requests.single().accept)
```

Parameters:

- `files: List<PantrixFile>`: what a user chooses at a pick, until the test gives others.

Members:

- `requests: List<FilePickRequest>`: Every pick asked for since the picker was made, in order: the kinds of file it showed and how many it took.

### TestFileSaver

`import com.pantrixui.testing.TestFileSaver`, from `com.pantrixui:testing`

```kotlin
class TestFileSaver(
    public var result: FileSaveResult = FileSaveResult.Saved
) : FileSaver
```

A file saver of the test's own: it keeps every file it is given, as a user who chooses a place for each, and answers with `result`. `PantrixTestTheme` gives one of its own to the screen in the place of the platform's, so that no window for saving opens and nothing is written to the machine; a test that reads what was saved gives its own, inside the theme.

```kotlin
val saver = TestFileSaver()
setContent {
    PantrixTestTheme { CompositionLocalProvider(LocalFileSaver provides saver) { ThemeBuilderScreen() } }

assertEquals(listOf("Theme.kt"), saver.files.map { it.name })
```

Parameters:

- `result: FileSaveResult`: what each save answers: saved, unless the test makes the user cancel or the place fail.

Members:

- `files: List<PantrixFile>`: Every file given to be saved since the saver was made, in order.

# com.pantrixui:material3: the API no page documents

The bridge between Pantrix UI's theme and Material 3's, in both directions.

## Package com.pantrixui.material3

### ColorScheme.toPantrixColors

`import com.pantrixui.material3.toPantrixColors`, from `com.pantrixui:material3`

```kotlin
fun ColorScheme.toPantrixColors(base: PantrixColors = pantrixColorsAsDarkAs(this)): PantrixColors
```

Pantrix's colours from this Material scheme: what Pantrix's components are drawn in inside a Material app, so that a screen written with them reads as the app's other screens do.

Each colour Material has a role for comes from the scheme. The brand's role is Material's primary, the neutral one its secondary, and danger its error. The backdrop is the scheme's background and a raised surface its `surfaceContainerLow`, which stands forward of the background as a card does in Material. The text is drawn in the scheme's `onBackground` and `onSurfaceVariant`, and the edges in its `outline` and `outlineVariant`.

What Material has no role for comes from `base`: the success, info and warning roles, the edge under a pointer, the focus ring, the colours of what is disabled, the chart's colours, and how much the scrim dims.

Parameters:

- `base: PantrixColors`: the Pantrix colours for what the scheme has none of: Pantrix's own by default, as dark as the scheme. `pantrixColorsAsDarkAs`: Pantrix's own colours as dark as `scheme`: the dark set when its background is.

### PantrixColors.toColorScheme

`import com.pantrixui.material3.toColorScheme`, from `com.pantrixui:material3`

```kotlin
fun PantrixColors.toColorScheme(): ColorScheme
```

A Material scheme from these Pantrix colours: what Material's components are drawn in inside a Pantrix app, so that a component Pantrix does not have reads as Pantrix's own do.

The brand's role is Material's primary, the neutral role its secondary, the info role its tertiary and danger its error; each of them gives its fixed colours too, from its container. The scheme's surface is the backdrop, as in Material's own schemes, and its containers step from the raised surface towards the text: `surfaceContainerLow` is the surface, and each container after it lays a little more of the text's colour over it. `outline` is the mark of a control, and `outlineVariant` the edge of a box: Material draws an outlined button, a chip and an outlined card in it, so they stand out as clearly as Pantrix's own fields and chips. Material's dividers take that edge too, a step stronger than Pantrix's.

Material's scrim is opaque, and its components dim with it as they need; the one given is these colours' scrim at full strength.

### Shapes.toPantrixShapes

`import com.pantrixui.material3.toPantrixShapes`, from `com.pantrixui:material3`

```kotlin
fun Shapes.toPantrixShapes(base: PantrixShapes = PantrixShapes()): PantrixShapes
```

Pantrix's corner radii from Material's shape scale, each step from the Material step of its radius: extra small, small, medium and large become `sm`, `md`, `lg` and `xl`, so that Material's own scale, 4, 8, 12 and 16dp, gives Pantrix's own, and a Pantrix component is as round in a Material app as in its own theme. Pantrix's `xs`, less round than any Material step, comes from `base`; Material's extra large, rounder than any Pantrix step, has no Pantrix step. Square and fully round are the same in both.

Parameters:

- `base: PantrixShapes`: the shapes Material has no step for: Pantrix's own by default.

### PantrixShapes.toMaterialShapes

`import com.pantrixui.material3.toMaterialShapes`, from `com.pantrixui:material3`

```kotlin
fun PantrixShapes.toMaterialShapes(fallback: Shapes = Shapes()): Shapes
```

Material's shape scale from Pantrix's corner radii, each step from the Pantrix step of its radius: `sm`, `md`, `lg` and `xl` become extra small, small, medium and large, so that Pantrix's own scale gives Material's own from extra small to large. Material's extra large, rounder than any Pantrix step, takes `xl`, the roundest.

Material takes shapes made of corners only. A Pantrix step of another shape, a brand's own outline, takes `fallback`'s shape for that step.

Parameters:

- `fallback: Shapes`: the shapes for the steps whose Pantrix shape is not made of corners: Material's own by default.

### PantrixThemeFromMaterial

`import com.pantrixui.material3.PantrixThemeFromMaterial`, from `com.pantrixui:material3`

```kotlin
@Composable
fun PantrixThemeFromMaterial(content: @Composable () -> Unit)
```

A Pantrix theme made of the Material theme around it: inside a Material app, Pantrix's components in `content` take its colours, its type scale and its shapes, so that a screen moved to Pantrix reads as the app's other screens do.

The colours are `toPantrixColors` of the scheme, as dark as it; the type is `toPantrixTypography` over Pantrix's own scale; the shapes are `toPantrixShapes`. Everything else is Pantrix's own, or what a `PantrixTheme` inside gives.

At its root, Pantrix's text style is the one a Material text takes there, the scheme's large body. Its content colour stays Pantrix's own, which on the theme's grounds is already the scheme's text colour: at a Material theme's root Material's own is its default black, which only a Material surface replaces. Inside a Material surface, `PantrixContentFromMaterial` gives Pantrix's content the surface's colour.

Where it is the outermost Pantrix theme, it makes what the system draws follow the scheme's dark rather than the system's: Android's bars' icons, iOS's status bar, keyboard and controls. A Material app that sets them itself gives the other form `followSystemBars = false`.

Parameters:

- `content: @Composable () -> Unit`

### PantrixThemeFromMaterial

`import com.pantrixui.material3.PantrixThemeFromMaterial`, from `com.pantrixui:material3`

```kotlin
@Composable
fun PantrixThemeFromMaterial(
    followSystemBars: Boolean,
    content: @Composable () -> Unit
)
```

`PantrixThemeFromMaterial`, told whether it sets what the system draws.

Parameters:

- `followSystemBars: Boolean`: whether this theme, where it is the outermost Pantrix theme, makes what the system draws follow the scheme's dark rather than the system's: Android's bars' icons, iOS's status bar, keyboard and controls. A Material app that sets them itself, or whose bars are coloured, turns it off. docs/guide/system-bars/SYSTEM_BARS_GUIDE.md has the whole of it.
- `content: @Composable () -> Unit`: what takes the theme: Pantrix's components inside the Material app.

### MaterialThemeFromPantrix

```kotlin
@Composable
fun MaterialThemeFromPantrix(content: @Composable () -> Unit)
```

A Material theme made of the Pantrix theme around it: inside a Pantrix app, Material's components in `content` take its colours, its type scale and its shapes, so that a component Pantrix does not have reads as Pantrix's own do.

The scheme is `toColorScheme` of Pantrix's colours, the type scale `toMaterialTypography` and the shapes `toMaterialShapes`.

At its root, Material's content colour and text style are the ones a Pantrix text would take there: `MaterialContentFromPantrix`.

```kotlin

fun MaterialContentFromPantrix(content: @Composable () -> Unit)
```

Gives Material's text and icons in `content` the colour and the style a Pantrix text takes where this stands: what Material's content on a Pantrix surface or fill is wrapped in, so that it reads there as Pantrix's does. Where nothing gives Pantrix a content colour, it is the theme's text colour.

### Typography.toPantrixTypography

`import com.pantrixui.material3.toPantrixTypography`, from `com.pantrixui:material3`

```kotlin
fun Typography.toPantrixTypography(base: PantrixTypography): PantrixTypography
```

Pantrix's type scale from this Material one: what Pantrix's text is set in inside a Material app.

Each Pantrix role takes the Material style of its size: display the small display (36 in Material's own scale), headline the medium headline (28), title the large title (22), body the large body (16), label the large label (14), footnote the small body (12) and caption the small label (11). Material has no style of a callout's size: the callout is the large body's face and weight at `base`'s callout size. Nor has it a monospace style: the code is `base`'s.

Parameters:

- `base: PantrixTypography`: the Pantrix scale the callout's size and the code come from.

### PantrixTypography.toMaterialTypography

`import com.pantrixui.material3.toMaterialTypography`, from `com.pantrixui:material3`

```kotlin
fun PantrixTypography.toMaterialTypography(): Typography
```

A Material type scale from this Pantrix one: what Material's text is set in inside a Pantrix app.

Each Material style takes the Pantrix role of its size, and where Pantrix has no role that large, its largest: the three displays are the display, the large and the medium headline the headline, the small headline and the large title the title, the medium title and the large body the body, the small title, the medium body and the large label the label, the small body and the medium label the footnote, and the small label the caption. Material's emphasized styles are its plain ones, as Material's own scale gives them for a scale of an app's.
